---
title: "Global filtering"
format: html
editor: visual
---

A global filtering is typically applied early to preserve only relevant taxonomic assignations and remove very low-count OTUs that are disproportionately driven by sequencing/PCR error and index misassignment, thereby reducing noise and improving downstream compositional and multivariate analyses.

This section documents how to filter OTUs based on taxonomic assignations, how to explore the abundance and prevalence of OTUs, and how to filter out singletons and rare OTUs based on absolute or relative abundance thresholds in `phyloseq` objects. To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `004_global_filter.R` and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
library(downloadthis)
library(plotly)
library(phyloseq)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggpubr)
library(microViz)
load("../../../RData/ITS/otu_ctrl_clean.RData")
```

```{r}
#| layout: [[-10,35,-5,40,-10]]

download_file(

load("RData/ITS/otu_ctrl_clean.RData")
```

## Taxonomy filtering

This first simple step serves to preserve only the relevant OTUs that were targeted with each primer sets: i.e., Bacteria for 16S, Fungi for ITS and Metazoa for CO1.

Note that the 16S primers amplifying the V4-V5 regions are also suitable for Archaea. The choice to include them or not in the following filtering depends on the hypotheses of your study. Similarly, primers targeting the internal transcribed spacer (ITS1 and ITS2) regions, while commonly used as the universal barcoding marker for fungi, often co-amplify DNA from a wide variety of other Eukaryotes due to the conserved nature of the flanking ribosomal RNA genes (18S, 5.8S, and 28S). For example, DNA from plants and protists is often amplified using these primers. It is recommended to filter them out when the hypotheses of the study are focused on Fungi. Finally, CO1 primers may also amplify Prokaryotes or other Eukaryotes, but these are not specificly targeted and should be filtered out.

+----------+------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+-----------+--------------+---------------------------+
| Name     | Target                             | Primers (sequence 5’-3’)                | Regions   | Length       | References                |
+==========+====================================+=========================================+===========+==============+===========================+
| 16S      | Prokaryotes (Bacteria and Archaea) | 515F-Y (GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA)\           | V4-V5     | 360-500 bp\  | [@parada2015]             |
|          |                                    | 926RB (CCGYCAATTYMTTTRAGTTT)            |           | (\~460 bp)   |                           |
+----------+------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+-----------+--------------+---------------------------+
| ITS      | Fungi                              | ITS9MUN (TGTACACACCGCCCGTCG)\           | ITS1-ITS2 | 150-1200 bp\ | [@tedersoo2016]           |
|          |                                    | ITS4ngsUni (CCTSCSCTTANTDATATGC)        |           | (\~280 bp)   |                           |
+----------+------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+-----------+--------------+---------------------------+
| CO1      | Metazoa                            | mlCOIintF (GGWACWGGWTGAACWGTWTAYCCYCC)\ | 320-345\  | 250-700\     | [@leray2013; @geller2013] |
|          |                                    | jgHCO2198 (TAIACYTCIGGRTGICCRAARAAYCA)  | 658       | (\~313 bp)   |                           |
+----------+------------------------------------+-----------------------------------------+-----------+--------------+---------------------------+

: Table 1. Primer sets used for this data set

This demonstration is done with the ITS data, and we choose to keep only Fungi.

```{r}
#| output: false
# Select organisms that should be included in the analysis
otu_table_tax <- subset_taxa(otu_ctrl_clean, kingdom == "Fungi")

# Count OTUs before and after filtering
ntaxa(otu_ctrl_clean) # 16687
ntaxa(otu_table_tax) # 9043 (~46% of the OTUs were not Fungi)

# How many reads were removed?
sum(sample_sums(otu_ctrl_clean)) - sum(sample_sums(otu_table_tax)) # 69358 reads
sum(sample_sums(otu_table_tax)) # 360336 reads belong to Fungi
```

In this demonstration, \~46% of the OTUs (and \~16% of the reads) were not Fungi. The ITS primers also amplify many other eukaryotes (e.g., Alveolata, Rhizaria, Amoebozoa, Metazoa and plants), as well as the synthetic spike-in of the positive controls (kingdom `Unispike1`, see [Dealing with positive controls](../controls-positive.qmd)). These are all removed here.

Which organisms to preserve or to remove from your data set depends on your sample type (e.g., soil vs water), the origin of your sample (e.g., tropical vs arctic) and your research question. Note that each genetic marker needs its own taxonomy filter. For example, the 16S primers also amplify chloroplasts and mitochondria, which contain DNA similar to bacteria because they are ancestral bacteria. In the databases used to BLAST the 16S marker, chloroplasts are assigned at the order level and mitochondria at the family level, both within the kingdom Bacteria, and must be removed separately:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# 16S only: remove chloroplasts and mitochondria
otu_table_tax <- subset_taxa(otu_ctrl_clean, kingdom == "Bacteria")
otu_table_tax <- subset_taxa(otu_table_tax, order != "Chloroplast" &
                               family != "Mitochondria")
```

## Explore the abundance and prevalence of OTUs

Sequencing data sets are characterized by a long tail of rare OTUs, i.e., OTUs represented by a low number of reads. Some of them may be products of sequencing errors that were not removed by the bioinformatic pipeline. Are they real? Is their presence meaningful in our analysis? It is often hard to decide which cutoff to use for an OTU to be considered "real", and the choice is often a bit arbitrary. It is therefore important to explore the data before deciding.

### Number of reads per OTU

Some OTUs have 0 reads at this stage: they were only present in the control samples, which were removed in the previous step. We exclude them from the exploration.

```{r}
#| output: false
# Remove the OTUs with 0 reads (only present in the controls)
otu_table_explore <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_tax) > 0, otu_table_tax)

# Total number of reads per OTU
reads_otu <- data.frame(reads = taxa_sums(otu_table_explore))

min(reads_otu$reads) # 1 read
max(reads_otu$reads) # 16793 reads

# How many OTUs have more than 1000 reads?
sum(reads_otu$reads > 1000) # 58 OTUs
```

```{r}
# Plot the distribution of the number of reads per OTU (log scale)
ggplot(reads_otu, aes(x = reads)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Number of reads per OTU (log10 scale)", y = "Number of OTUs") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Most OTUs have a low number of reads, and only a few OTUs (58) are very abundant, with more than 1000 reads.

### Prevalence of OTUs

The prevalence of an OTU is the number of samples in which it is present. To calculate it, we first convert the OTU table to presence-absence.

```{r}
#| output: false
# Convert the OTU table to presence-absence (1 = present, 0 = absent)
otu_table_pa <- transform_sample_counts(otu_table_explore, function(x) 1 * (x > 0))

# Number of OTUs per sample
sample_sums(otu_table_pa)

# Number of samples in which each OTU is present (prevalence)
prev_otu <- data.frame(prevalence = taxa_sums(otu_table_pa))

# How many OTUs are present in only one or two samples?
sum(prev_otu$prevalence == 1) # 4843 OTUs
sum(prev_otu$prevalence == 2) # 1367 OTUs
```

```{r}
# Plot the distribution of the prevalence of OTUs
ggplot(prev_otu, aes(x = prevalence)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Prevalence of OTUs (number of samples)", y = "Number of OTUs") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Most OTUs occur in a very low number of samples: more than half of the fungal OTUs (4843) are found in a single sample. Filtering OTUs based on their prevalence would therefore lead to the loss of a large number of OTUs.

What if we remove the OTUs present in less than 10 samples?

```{r}
# Keep the OTUs present in at least 10 samples
prev_otu10 <- filter(prev_otu, prevalence >= 10)

ggplot(prev_otu10, aes(x = prevalence)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Prevalence of OTUs (number of samples)", y = "Number of OTUs") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Even after removing the OTUs present in less than 10 samples, the same pattern is observed: OTUs with a low prevalence are the most frequent. It is hard to choose a cutoff based on prevalence only. Let's look at filters based on the abundance of OTUs instead.

## Singletons and rare OTUs

Singletons and other rare OTUs are predominantly composed of PCR, sequencing, and chimera artefacts, and their removal has been shown to have negligible effects on hypothesis-driven community comparisons while substantially reducing noise [@edgar2016; @nikodemova2023; @sgarbi2020; @cao2021]. Retaining them is mainly justified in studies explicitly targeting rare biosphere diversity and requires careful validation [@brown2015].

In R, singletons are typically removed by excluding OTUs with a total count of one across all samples, while rare OTUs are filtered by applying absolute (e.g. total counts \<5 or \<10) or relative abundance thresholds (e.g. \<0.01%) to the OTU table [@edgar2016; @brown2015; @nikodemova2023], commonly using `phyloseq::prune_taxa()` in combination with `taxa_sums()`.

### Removing singletons

Removing singletons is as simple as keeping anything that has more than 1 read throughout the entire data set.

```{r}
#| output: false
# Remove singletons
otu_table_single <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_tax) > 1, otu_table_tax)

# Count OTUs after filtering
ntaxa(otu_table_single) # 5825 (~36% of the fungal OTUs were singletons)
```

In this data set, a large proportion of the OTUs (\~36%) are singletons, i.e., OTUs with a single read in the whole data set. Together, however, they represent less than 1% of the reads.

### Removing rare OTUs

OTUs are considered rare if their abundance is small compared to other OTUs. They may be present in many samples, but if their total sum across samples is smaller than *k*% of the average sequencing depth (relative abundance), or smaller than *k* reads (absolute abundance) then they are considered rare.

NOTE: When calculating the average sequencing depth, ignore controls and blanks, as they artificially lower the average.

#### Relative abundance

Typically, thresholds between 0.005% and 0.1% relative abundance are found in the literature. We define relative thresholds based on the average sequencing depth (assuming that all samples have sufficient sequencing depth).

```{r}
#| output: false
# Calculate the average sequencing depth
seq_depth_avg <- mean(sample_sums(otu_table_tax)) # 4048.7 reads

# Calculate thresholds based on k% of the average sequencing depth
# For the sake of this exercise, multiple thresholds between 0.05% and 1% are
# tested to compare their effects on various community analyses.
thresh05 <- ceiling(seq_depth_avg*0.05/100) # 3 reads
thresh1 <- ceiling(seq_depth_avg*0.1/100) # 5 reads
thresh10 <- ceiling(seq_depth_avg*1/100) # 41 reads
```

Because the sequencing depth of this ITS data set is low (\~4000 reads per sample), the lower thresholds found in the literature (0.005% or 0.01%) correspond to 1 read, i.e., they are identical to removing singletons. For the sake of this demonstration, we have therefore tested thresholds of 0.05% and 0.1%, as well as a threshold up to 1% to better illustrate the effects of filtering out rare OTUs on different community analyses. With a deeper sequencing (e.g., \~140000 reads per sample, typical of 16S data sets), the same percentages correspond to many more reads (0.005% = 7 reads, 0.01% = 14 reads).

```{r}
#| output: false
# Remove all OTUs that have a total sum lower than the threshold
otu_table_rare05 <- otu_table_tax %>% prune_taxa(taxa_sums(.) > thresh05, .)
otu_table_rare1 <- otu_table_tax %>% prune_taxa(taxa_sums(.) > thresh1, .)
otu_table_rare10 <- otu_table_tax %>% prune_taxa(taxa_sums(.) > thresh10, .)

# Compare the number of OTU in each filtering step
ntaxa(otu_ctrl_clean) #16687 (before filtering)
ntaxa(otu_table_tax) #9043 (~54% of OTUs are Fungi)
ntaxa(otu_table_single) #5825 (~36% singletons)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare05) #3597 (~60% of OTUs have 3 reads or less; 0.05%)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare1) #2763 (~69% of OTUs have 5 reads or less; 0.1%)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare10) #787 (~91% of OTUs have 41 reads or less; 1%)
```

#### Absolute abundance

Typically, thresholds between 5-10 reads are found in the literature. In this example, a threshold of 5 reads corresponds to a relative abundance threshold of 0.1%. If the average sequencing depth of your data set is larger than the one presented here, it may be relevant to test removing 5 and 10 reads if those absolute thresholds are significantly lower than a relative threshold at 0.005%.

#### Compare thresholds

To visualize the effect of these different thresholds, we must first create a data frame per filtered OTU table that summarizes the sequencing depth per sample and the Observed OTU (richness).

```{r}
#| output: false
# Non-filtered OTU table
seq_depth_raw <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_tax)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_tax, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_tax)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "raw")

# Singletons
seq_depth_single <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_single)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_single, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_single)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "singletons")

# Rare 0.05% (<=3 reads)
seq_depth_rare05 <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rare05)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_rare05, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_rare05)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "rare 0.05%")

# Rare 0.1% (<=5 reads)
seq_depth_rare1 <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rare1)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_rare1, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_rare1)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "rare 0.1%")

# Rare 1% (<=41 reads)
seq_depth_rare10 <- cbind.data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rare10)) %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_rare10, measures = "Observed")) %>%
  mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(otu_table_rare10)) %>%
  arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
  mutate(seq_depth = "rare 1%")

# Combine data frames
seq_depth_all <- seq_depth_raw %>% rbind(seq_depth_single) %>%
  rbind(seq_depth_rare05) %>% rbind(seq_depth_rare1) %>%
  rbind(seq_depth_rare10)
```

##### Effect on library size

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Plot the library size of all samples
ggplot(seq_depth_all, aes(x = Index, y = LibrarySize, color = seq_depth)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_ly(data = seq_depth_all, x = ~Index, y = ~LibrarySize, color = ~seq_depth,
        type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers+lines', colors = 'Dark2',
        text = ~paste("Library Size: ", LibrarySize,
                      '<br>Sample ID: ', Soil_ID))
```

With this analysis, we can see that removing singletons barely affects library size, as the points almost completely overlap with the non-filtered data, even though we lost \~36% of the OTUs. In addition, filtering rare OTUs at a threshold of 0.1% or less (5 reads or less) changes very little in the library size, even though we lost \~69% of the OTUs. Only the threshold of 1% removes a substantial number of reads.

::: callout-tip
Try zooming in on a selection of points with large library size (e.g., the samples with an `Index` above 80) to better see the effects of the different thresholds.
:::

##### Effect on OTU richness

To confirm our choice of the best filtering threshold, let's compare the effect of filtering on OTU richness.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Plot the OTU richness of all samples
ggplot(seq_depth_all, aes(x = Index, y = Observed, color = seq_depth)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_ly(data = seq_depth_all, x = ~Index, y = ~Observed, color = ~seq_depth,
        type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers+lines', colors = 'Dark2',
        text = ~paste("Library Size: ", LibrarySize,
                      "<br>Observed OTU: ", Observed,
                      '<br>Sample ID: ', Soil_ID))
```

This plot shows that every filtering step lowers the OTU richness of the samples, especially in the samples with a large library size. The thresholds up to 0.1% return the same pattern of OTU richness as a function of library size, whereas the threshold of 1% flattens the differences between samples.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# Add the Shannon index to the combined data frame
otu_tables <- list("raw" = otu_table_tax, "singletons" = otu_table_single,
                   "rare 0.05%" = otu_table_rare05, "rare 0.1%" = otu_table_rare1,
                   "rare 1%" = otu_table_rare10)
seq_depth_all <- lapply(names(otu_tables), function(x) {
  ps <- otu_tables[[x]]
  cbind.data.frame(sample_data(ps)) %>%
    cbind(estimate_richness(ps, measures = c("Observed", "Shannon"))) %>%
    mutate(LibrarySize = sample_sums(ps)) %>%
    arrange(LibrarySize) %>% mutate(Index = row_number()) %>%
    mutate(seq_depth = x)
}) %>% bind_rows()
```

::: callout-tip
Try comparing other alpha diversity indices, such as the Shannon index.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Add Shannon index to each OTU table as such
seq_depth_raw <- seq_depth_raw %>%
  cbind(estimate_richness(otu_table_tax, measures = "Shannon"))

# Plot the Shannon index of all samples
ggplot(seq_depth_all, aes(x = Index, y = Shannon, color = seq_depth)) +
  geom_point() + geom_line()
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_ly(data = seq_depth_all, x = ~Index, y = ~Shannon, color = ~seq_depth,
        type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers+lines', colors = 'Dark2',
        text = ~paste("Library Size: ", LibrarySize,
                      "<br>Shannon index: ", round(Shannon, 2),
                      '<br>Sample ID: ', Soil_ID))
```

Filtering rare OTUs has little effect on the Shannon index, which gives more weight to abundant OTUs. Note also the lack of a clear relationship between the Shannon index and library size.
:::

##### Effect on beta diversity

To confirm our choice of filtering further, we can compare how the different filtering methods affect beta diversity.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
# Non-filtered OTU table
beta_div_raw <- otu_table_tax %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Singletons
beta_div_single <- otu_table_single %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Rare 0.05%
beta_div_rare05 <- otu_table_rare05 %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Rare 0.1%
beta_div_rare1 <- otu_table_rare1 %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Rare 1%
beta_div_rare10 <- otu_table_rare10 %>%
  tax_transform("identity", rank = "taxa_OTU") %>%
  dist_calc("aitchison") %>%
  ord_calc("PCoA") %>%
  ord_plot(color = "Land_use", auto_caption = NA) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = Land_use))

# Visualize all plots together
ggarrange(beta_div_raw, beta_div_single, beta_div_rare05, beta_div_rare1,
          beta_div_rare10,
          labels = c(
            "Non-filtered (9043 OTUs)", "Singletons (5825 OTUs)",
            "0.05% (<=3 reads; 3597 OTUs)", "0.1% (<=5 reads; 2763 OTUs)",
            "1% (<=41 reads; 787 OTUs)"),
          ncol = 3, nrow = 2, common.legend = TRUE,
          hjust = 0, label.x = 0.2, font.label = list(size = 10))
```

With this analysis, we can see that the overall patterns are the same with all filtering thresholds: the agricultural sites and the grassland separate from the oak forests. Note that the orientation of the axes is arbitrary: an axis may simply be flipped from one plot to the other.

Overall, these plots showed that rare OTUs were mostly found in samples with a large library size, and that filtering out rare OTUs does not affect the main patterns. Only a threshold as high as 1% considerably affected the richness of the samples.

#### Choosing the best threshold

Ultimately, the choice of the "best" threshold is completely arbitrary. Various thresholds are found in the literature and no one is more justified than another. As a reminder: singletons and other rare OTUs have been previously found to be predominantly composed of artefacts, thus, their removal has been shown to have negligible effects on hypothesis-driven community comparisons while substantially reducing noise [@edgar2016; @nikodemova2023; @sgarbi2020; @cao2021]. Retaining them is only justified in studies explicitly targeting rare biosphere diversity and requires careful validation [@brown2015].

So, is it necessary to filter rare OTUs? As seen in this demonstration, removing rare OTUs mainly lowers the richness of the samples, and has little effect on the community composition. In this workflow, we keep all fungal OTUs (no abundance filter), for two reasons:

1.  Rare OTUs, and singletons in particular, are needed to estimate the number of undetected OTUs in each sample (extrapolated richness, see [Alpha diversity](../../stats/alpha-div.qmd)). Removing them would bias these estimates.
2.  The sequencing depth of this data set is low, so that even the lowest thresholds remove a large proportion of the OTUs.

We only remove the OTUs with 0 reads (only present in the controls).

```{r}
#| output: false
# Keep all fungal OTUs, but remove the OTUs with 0 reads
otu_table_rare <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(otu_table_tax) > 0, otu_table_tax)
ntaxa(otu_table_rare) # 9039 OTUs
```

To use a filtering threshold instead, replace the line above with, e.g., `otu_table_rare <- otu_table_single` (remove singletons) or `otu_table_rare <- otu_table_rare05` (remove OTUs with 3 reads or less).

::: callout-important
If you decide to filter rare OTUs in your own data, report the threshold you used, and check that it does not change your conclusions.
:::

### Save the OTU tables

```{r}
#| eval: false
# OTU table with taxonomy filtered
save(otu_table_tax, file = "RData/ITS/otu_taxa_clean.RData")

# OTU table with singletons filtered
save(otu_table_single, file = "RData/ITS/otu_single_clean.RData")

# OTU table with rare taxa filtered
save(otu_table_rare, file = "RData/ITS/otu_rare_clean.RData")
```
